source.title: Generalisation error in learning with random features and the hidden manifold model
source.authors: Federica Gerace; Bruno Loureiro; Florent Krzakala; M. M'ezard; Lenka Zdeborov'a

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates double-descent curves for random-feature generalized linear models, using a replica analysis rather than testing the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results include test-error sweeps over feature count and sample count, and report where the interpolation peak occurs. Training-loss behavior at the peak is described in the text but is not separately rowed because the claim versions concern test error. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as findings here. The projection-quality comparison in Fig. 5 is mentioned under fits_no_version because it compares Gaussian and orthogonal projections, not a claim version.
record.test_reason: Replica-method theory with simulations derives test-error curves for random-feature and hidden-manifold GLMs. It reports double-descent peaks over feature count (square and logistic loss) and over sample count, and how regularization changes peak height. It uses a different method and model class from the originals but targets the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main contribution is a replica-derived closed-form generalization error for GLMs on random-feature and hidden-manifold data, with a Gaussian-equivalence result. Applications show: logistic double descent peaking at linear separability rather than p=n; orthogonal projections beating Gaussian; and a hidden-manifold phase diagram where the peak shrinks with regularization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses replica-method asymptotics and simulations on synthetic random-feature and hidden-manifold generalized linear models, rather than the original deep-network scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The peak location depends on loss and data separability; it varies with n/d. The peak height changes with ridge regularization. Gaussian and orthogonal projections have different separation behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: For logistic loss the peak is not at p=n but at the linear-separability threshold, which shifts with n/d (α*=2 as n/d→0) and with the projection type.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size-wise peak location is set by a loss-specific interpolation threshold (zero training loss), not by raw parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonal and structured random projections outperform Gaussian ones and reach the kernel limit with fewer features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In random-feature models, orthogonal projections generalize better than Gaussian projections.

record.problems: The replica calculation is described as non-rigorous and is conjectured to be exact; the evidence uses synthetic high-dimensional models rather than deep networks. Simulation results are presented without reported error bars or confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. Fig. 5 projection comparisons are included as curves for the tested double-descent behavior; their separate projection-performance comparison is summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: No deep networks trained while scaling size.
Only a synthetic hidden-manifold task with square loss; no other data, losses or deep models.
Only random-feature / hidden-manifold GLMs (Gaussian, orthogonal, Hadamard, DCT projections); no other model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure tested across size, epochs and samples.
Label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, and whether the peak fully disappears at optimal λ are not reported in the text.

missing.what: Theory-vs-simulation curve (d=200) for logistic loss, λ=10^-3, n/d=3, showing generalization and training error vs p/n. This is the simulation evidence for the double-descent curve.
Optimal-λ learning curve on the sample axis; error saturates at about 0.0325 for large α. Whether the peak vanishes is not stated.
Kernel-limit errors at optimal λ: about 0.17 (square loss) vs 0.16 (logistic loss); logistic is better except near its peak.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are figure-only; curves are theory, with simulations shown agreeing. The replica formula is non-rigorous but reproduces Mei–Montanari for ridge with Gaussian features. Several optimal-λ rows were relinked from V4 to V6 as cannot_determine, since the text never describes their shape. The reader's V6 'limits_scope' was changed to 'supports'; the lack of a disappearance result is an untested part, not a contrary result.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test deep networks while scaling model size.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The sample-size sweep is for a synthetic hidden-manifold classification task with square loss and ridge regularization, not other data or learning settings.
Tests random-feature generalized linear models and projection matrices, not a broad survey of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The effect of label noise, triple or multiple descent, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that turns the curve into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.reason: Error peaks at the interpolation threshold, where training loss hits zero (p/n=1 for square loss, the linear-separability point for logistic), then decreases with more features (R1, R2, R5, R6, R9, R10, R13, R14).
relationships.display_finding: Error peaked where training loss reached zero, at p/n=1 for square loss and the separability threshold for logistic loss, then decreased with additional features.
